subtype: Approach: thinking of the pet as a family member with rights [Thinking]
passage: Behind the village school, Tushar called across the field, "One more game, Aadhya! The sun is still up." Aadhya looked at the long shadows. She thought of Moti, her dog, lying by the gate since noon with his chin on his paws. "Food and water is not everything," she thought. "He needs a walk and someone to sit with him. He is not a stone." "I can't stay," she called back. "Moti is waiting." Tushar shrugged, a little disappointed. She ran home, and Moti jumped up so fast that he knocked his bowl over.

qa.q: Where had Moti been lying since noon?
qa.a: Moti had been lying by the gate.

qa.q: What was Aadhya thinking as she looked at the long shadows?
qa.a: She was concerned that Moti was lonely and needed her company, not only food.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya do so that both the game and Moti are looked after, and why?
qa.a: She could bring Moti to the field or fix a walk right after the game, so her friends and her dog both get time.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel when Aadhya leaves?
qa.a: Tushar is a little disappointed, as his shrug shows, since he wanted one more game.

grounding: A girl reasons that her dog needs walks and company as well as food, and tells her friends she must go home.

subtype: Approach: thinking of the pet as a family member with rights [Thinking]
passage: The snow had melted in Sapporo, and after school Aiko wanted to stay at the park until the lamps came on. "One more round of tag, Yuki!" Yuki checked the clock tower. Half past four. She thought of Kuro, their old dog, lying by the door since morning with only his food bowl for company. "Food isn't the whole thing," she thought. "If someone fed me and left me alone all day, I'd go strange too." She told Aiko, "I can't. Kuro's been alone all day. He needs his walk, and he needs someone to talk to." Aiko pouted. "He's a dog." "He's our dog," Yuki said, picking up her bag. At home, Kuro's tail thumped against the floor before she even opened the door.

qa.q: What time did Yuki see on the clock tower?
What was Yuki thinking about Kuro?
qa.a: She felt concerned for Kuro, alone all day, and reasoned that he needs walks and company, not just food.

qa.q: What else could Yuki try so she can still play sometimes?
qa.a: Bring Kuro to the park with her friends, so he gets his walk and she still gets her game.

qa.q: How does Aiko see Yuki leaving?
qa.a: Aiko pouts, disappointed, and seems to think a dog should not come before play.

grounding: A girl reasons that her dog needs walks and company as well as food, so she leaves the park early.

subtype: Approach: thinking of the pet as a family member with rights [Thinking]
passage: At the end of badminton practice at the sports club, the coach said the court was free till seven for anyone who wanted to stay. Pooja was already bouncing. "Parul, doubles! Come on!" Parul looked at the big clock over the scoreboard. Six. Both her parents worked late on Thursdays. Lucky had been in the flat since two, with food and water but nobody to lean against. "He eats fine," she thought, "but he's a dog, not a plant. He needs a walk and someone around." She zipped her racket bag. "Not today, Pooja. Lucky's waiting, and he's been alone all afternoon." Pooja groaned, then said, "Saturday, then?" "Saturday morning. I'll bring him to watch."

qa.q: When do both of Parul's parents work late?
What was Parul feeling as she zipped her bag?
qa.a: A little sorry to miss doubles, but responsible and sure Lucky needed her.

qa.q: What else could Parul arrange for Thursdays?
qa.a: She could ask a neighbour to take Lucky for a short walk, so she can sometimes stay late.
Pooja groans at first, then accepts and suggests Saturday instead.

grounding: A girl turns down extra play at the club because her dog needs a walk and company, not just food.
